concepts.name: Standard state of a solute
concepts.statement: For a solution the standard state is defined by the solute's infinite-dilution behavior: a hypothetical solution of 1 mol/L in which the solute still behaves as at infinite dilution, its particles not interacting with each other, so that the activity coefficient describes all the nonideal behavior where it is not equal to 1.

concepts.name: Activity coefficient from the vapor pressure
concepts.statement: The partial pressure of a component over a solution is P_i = a_iP_i*, so comparing with Raoult's law the activity coefficient is γ_i = P_i/(x_iP_i*) = P_i/P_i^R, the measured partial pressure over the one Raoult's law predicts: larger than one for a positive deviation, smaller than one for a negative one, and one for an ideal solution. Measuring the partial pressure of the vapor over a nonideal solution gives it from the phase diagram.

concepts.name: Colligative property
concepts.statement: A property that depends on the number of particles rather than their total mass, which is why it can be used to measure molar mass: melting point depression, boiling point elevation and osmotic pressure.

concepts.name: Solvent activity at the freezing point
concepts.statement: When a solution whose solid is pure solvent freezes, the solvent's chemical potentials in the solid and the solution are equal, μ₁ˢ = μ₁^liq* + RT ln a₁, so −Δμ₁/RT = ln a₁, and the Gibbs–Helmholtz relation turns this into ∂ln a₁/∂T = Δ_fus H̄₁/RT²; integrating that quantity determines activities.

concepts.name: Melting point depression
concepts.statement: A dilute solution whose solvent follows Raoult's law and whose solid holds no solute melts below the pure solvent: integrating ∂ln a₁/∂T from T_m* to T_m with ln a₁ = ln x₁ ≈ −x₂ gives −x₂ ≈ Δ_fus H̄₁(−ΔT)/(RT_m*²), often rewritten in molality as ΔT = K_f m.

concepts.name: Cryoscopic constant
concepts.statement: The solvent's constant K_f in ΔT = K_f m, the lowering of the melting point per unit molality of solute.

concepts.name: Finding a molar mass from the melting point depression
concepts.statement: With K_f known for the solvent, add a weighed amount of an unknown compound, measure the temperature depression to get the molality, and from the molality and the masses calculate the molar mass.

concepts.name: Boiling point elevation
concepts.statement: A nonvolatile solute raises the boiling point of the solvent, by reasoning quite similar to the melting point depression.

concepts.name: Semipermeable membrane
concepts.statement: A membrane permeable for some molecules but not for others, often by their size but also by their solubility in the barrier material; the walls of most plant and animal cells are one.

concepts.name: Osmosis
concepts.statement: When solvent molecules can pass through a membrane but solute molecules or ions cannot, solvent migrates spontaneously into the solution to increase its volume and reduce its concentration, much as an ideal gas expands against vacuum.

concepts.name: Osmotic pressure
concepts.statement: The hydrostatic pressure Π that builds up on the solution side as osmosis proceeds, under gravity in a U-shaped tube; at equilibrium it equalizes the flow of solvent through the membrane in both directions.

concepts.name: Osmotic equilibrium
concepts.statement: At equilibrium the pure solvent at P and the solution at P + Π have the same chemical potential, μ*(T, P) = μ*(T, P + Π) + RT ln a₁; integrating (∂μ*/∂P)_T = V̄₁* over the extra pressure turns this into ΠV̄₁* = −RT ln a₁.

concepts.name: Osmotic pressure of a dilute solution
concepts.statement: With the ideal approximation ln a₁ ≈ −x₂ the osmotic equilibrium gives RTx₂ = ΠV̄₁*, and with x₂ ≈ n₂/n₁ this becomes Π = RTc in the molar concentration of the solute.

concepts.name: Reverse osmosis
concepts.statement: Osmosis can be used in reverse: about 30 bar applied to sea water drives fresh water through a suitable membrane. Membranes clog easily and the water is not completely salt-free, so salt may accumulate on fields watered with it.

concepts.name: Finding a molar mass by osmometry
concepts.statement: Osmotic pressure is colligative, so measuring it for a known mass of dissolved solute gives the solute's molar mass, up to about 8000 daltons, where melting point depression and boiling point elevation reach only small molar masses.

concepts.name: Molar mass distribution of a polymer
concepts.statement: A polymer usually has a distribution of molar masses. It is dissolved and led over a size-exclusion column, and the effluent is probed against elution time by UV absorption (the monomer concentration) and by low angle laser light scattering or viscometry, which give different moments of the distribution; together they show how much material there is at each molar mass and how branched the chains are.

concepts.name: Purity from the melting behavior
concepts.statement: A slightly impure solid melts over a range, from a lower eutectic temperature up to its depressed melting point; in differential scanning calorimetry the melting peak skews toward lower temperatures as impurity grows, and modelling its shape with a modified melting point depression expression gives the total impurity level, a quality control in the pharmaceutical industry.

concepts.name: Nonideality of electrolyte solutions
concepts.statement: A strong electrolyte puts charged solutes into solution, whose interaction falls off as r⁻¹ rather than about r⁻⁶ for neutral species, so the solution diverges seriously from ideality even at very low concentrations.

concepts.name: Dissociation of a salt
concepts.statement: A salt C_ν₊A_ν₋ goes into solution as ν₊ cations of formal charge z₊ and ν₋ anions of charge z₋; ν₊ and ν₋ are the stoichiometric coefficients, ν = ν₊ + ν₋, and charge neutrality demands ν₊z₊ + ν₋z₋ = 0.

concepts.name: Chemical potential of a dissolved salt
concepts.statement: The dissociation makes the salt's chemical potential the sum over its ions, μ₂ = ν₊μ₊ + ν₋μ₋ with μ₂° = ν₊μ₊° + ν₋μ₋°, so ν₊ ln a₊ + ν₋ ln a₋ = ln a₂ and a₂ = a₊^ν₊ a₋^ν₋: the stoichiometric coefficients become exponents.

concepts.name: Mean ionic activity
concepts.statement: The activity a± defined by a±^ν ≡ a₂ = a₊^ν₊ a₋^ν₋: closely related to the salt's activity, but through an exponent, so a±² = a_NaCl and a±⁵ is the activity of Al₂(SO₄)₃.

concepts.name: Activity coefficients of the ions
concepts.statement: Working with molalities, each ion has an activity coefficient, a₊ = γ₊m₊ and a₋ = γ₋m₋, though neither can be determined separately, since one ion cannot be added without the other.

concepts.name: Molalities of the ions
concepts.statement: Stoichiometry relates the molalities of the ions to the molality m of the salt: m₊ = ν₊m and m₋ = ν₋m.

concepts.name: Mean ionic molality
concepts.statement: The molality m± defined by m±^ν ≡ m₊^ν₊ m₋^ν₋.

concepts.name: Activity of a salt from mean ionic quantities
concepts.statement: a₂ = a±^ν = γ±^ν m±^ν: the stoichiometry enters both the exponents and the molalities, so the activity of Al₂(SO₄)₃ is 108m⁵γ±⁵ and goes as the fifth power of its molality.

concepts.name: Measuring the mean ionic activity coefficient
concepts.statement: γ± can be determined: the water vapor pressure measured above the salt solution gives the osmotic coefficient φ, and the Gibbs–Duhem equation turns it into ln γ± (the book prints the integrand as [φ − 1]m′; it is (φ − 1)/m′). The salt's own negligible vapor pressure does not matter.

concepts.name: Ionic atmosphere
concepts.statement: Debye–Hückel theory treats the vicinity of each ion as an atmosphere-like cloud of charges of opposite sign that cancels the charge of the central ion, so from a distance the cloud looks neutral; its size depends on the concentration of all the other ions.

concepts.name: Debye length
concepts.statement: The size 1/κ of the ionic atmosphere, set by the ionic strength through κ² = constant · I, the constant holding e²N_A over ε_rε₀kT; the book calls κ itself the Debye-length.

concepts.name: Mean activity coefficient from the Debye length
concepts.statement: At sufficiently low concentrations ln γ± = −|q₊q₋|κ/(8πε_rε₀kT): the logarithm of the mean ionic activity coefficient is proportional to κ and so, for one salt, to the square root of its molality, and it depends on the ionic strength rather than the electrolyte's own concentration.

concepts.name: Distance of closest approach
concepts.statement: The parameter a₀ of the Debye–Hückel equation, the distance of closest approach of ions; in the extended equation it is the effective hydrated diameter a, about 3 Å for H⁺, Cl⁻, CN⁻ and HCOO⁻ and 9 Å for hydronium.

concepts.name: Extended Debye–Hückel equation
concepts.statement: log₁₀γ± = −Az²√I/(1 + Ba₀√I), with A = 0.51 and B = 3.29 nm⁻¹ (in mol^−1/2 dm^3/2) for water at 25 °C; at very low ionic strength the denominator is nearly one and the limiting law returns. Written with |z₊z₋| and the hydrated diameter a, it extends the limiting law to somewhat higher concentrations.

concepts.name: Holding the ionic strength constant
concepts.statement: Because the ionic strength involves every ion present, one ion can be replaced by a spectator of the same charge, Cu²⁺ by Zn²⁺ by diluting with a zinc solution of the same concentration, to lower its concentration while keeping the activity coefficients as nearly the same as possible.

concepts.name: Colloid
concepts.statement: A dispersion of solid particles of nanometre size, smaller than the wavelength of visible light, so the liquid stays clear, kept from precipitating because the particles are charged and wear an atmosphere of a certain Debye length that repels the others. Colloids are metastable, and a salt with highly charged ions can destabilize one by changing the ionic strength and so the Debye length.

concepts.name: Limits of Debye–Hückel theory
concepts.statement: The theory agrees with experiment below about 10⁻³ mol/L; beyond that its assumptions fail: ions associate, weak electrolytes are not fully dissociated, ions are neither point charges nor unpolarizable, the solvent is made of dipolar, polarizable molecules that solvate the ions, and the ionic radius becomes comparable to the atmosphere's. Most extensions are empirical, keeping the law at low concentration and adding terms in powers of the ionic strength.

concepts.name: Bjerrum length
concepts.statement: The separation at which the electrostatic interaction between two ions is comparable in magnitude to kT, which marks where ion association, followed up by Bjerrum, sets in.

concepts.name: Davies equation
concepts.statement: An empirical extension of Debye–Hückel theory, refined by fitting to data, for 25 °C: −log f± = 0.5z₁z₂(√I/(1 + √I) − 0.30I). The 0.30I term vanishes at low ionic strength, leaving Debye–Hückel, and grows at higher strength; for 1:1 electrolytes it is within about 2% at 0.1 M.

concepts.name: Pitzer equations
concepts.statement: Activity coefficients from a virial expansion of the excess Gibbs energy whose parameters characterize interactions among ions and solvent, thermodynamically rigorous at a given level of expansion; for the mean activity coefficient they agree with data to about 6 mol/kg.

concepts.name: Specific ion interaction theory
concepts.statement: SIT estimates single-ion activity coefficients at relatively high concentrations as the Debye–Hückel term plus interaction coefficients times the molalities of the other ions present; fitting equilibrium constants at several ionic strengths gives the coefficients and the constant at infinite dilution.
